title: None of them are actually seeds, and the fruit isn't a berry.
description:
None of them are actually seeds, and the fruit isn't a berry. Botanically, a strawberry fails the definition of a berry on every count that matters.

A strawberry's flower has dozens of separate ones. That single-ovary rule is why bananas, grapes, tomatoes and even cucumbers count as true berries, while strawberries, raspberries and blackberries don't.

It's the swollen base of the flower. What botanists call the receptacle grows large and fleshy around the true fruits, rather than the flesh coming from any ovary wall, which is how a true berry is built.

are the actual fruits, not seeds. Each dot is a separate dry fruit called an achene, and each one holds a single true seed sealed inside it.

The avocado, with its single huge seed, meets the botanical definition of a berry. The strawberry, with hundreds of visible seeds, doesn't.

Sources:
- https://www.britannica.com/science/berry-plant-reproductive-body - read in full 7 Sep 2026: Encyclopaedia Britannica, last updated 1 September 2026. Defines a true berry as a fleshy fruit produced from a single ovary, with the entire fruit wall present as edible flesh, and lists bananas, grapes, melons, oranges, tomatoes, cranberries and blueberries as true berries, while explicitly excluding raspberries, blackberries and strawberries from that category as they are not simple fruits from a single ovary; also covers the citrus hesperidium and the melon and cucumber pepo as further berry subtypes.
- https://sciencenotes.org/is-a-strawberry-a-berry-why-the-answer-is-surprisingly-no/ - read in full 7 Sep 2026: Science Notes (Anne Helmenstine, published 27 June 2026). Explains that a strawberry is an aggregate accessory fruit, meaning it develops from a flower with many separate ovaries rather than one, and that its edible red flesh is swollen flower receptacle tissue rather than tissue from any ovary wall; also explains that the surface dots are not seeds but individual dry fruits called achenes, each containing one true seed inside; and separately confirms the avocado is a true single-seeded berry by the botanical definition.
